body: Welcome. For roughly ninety days you will receive one short note a day to help you hold your views a little more lightly and change your mind with grace.
To begin, notice one opinion you hold very firmly. You do not have to question it yet; just see how certain it feels.
Changing your mind is not weakness. It is what a thoughtful person does when they learn something new.
Watch for the moment in a conversation when you stop listening and start preparing your reply. That is where open-mindedness slips.
Today, ask one person why they believe something, and listen to the whole answer before responding.
Notice how your body reacts when someone disagrees with you. A tight chest or hot face is a cue to slow down.
Try saying, I had not thought of it that way. It costs nothing and invites a better conversation.
Pick a belief you held five years ago that you no longer hold. What changed your mind? You have done this before.
Separate your ideas from your identity. You are not your opinions; you are the person who holds them, for now.
Read one article today from a source you usually avoid. You are not obliged to agree, only to understand.
When you feel the urge to win an argument, ask yourself whether you would rather be right or learn something.
Practise rating your certainty out of ten. Most views deserve a seven, not a ten.
Notice the people you dismiss before they finish speaking. What would it take to hear them out once?
Ask, what would change my mind about this? If the answer is nothing, that is worth noticing.
Admitting you were wrong often earns more respect than defending a weak position. Try it in a small matter this week.
Summarise someone else's view back to them until they say, yes, that is it. Only then share your own.
Curiosity is the antidote to defensiveness. Replace I disagree with tell me more, at least once today.
Think of an expert you trust who changed their position after new evidence. Changing course is how knowledge grows.
When you are tired or hungry, you will be more rigid. Save important disagreements for when you are rested.
Notice which topics make you instantly certain. Those are often the ones most worth examining.
Try steel-manning: describe the strongest version of a view you disagree with, as fairly as you can.
Pay attention to your sources. Do they ever tell you something you do not want to hear?
Changing your mind gracefully includes saying it out loud: I have thought about it, and I now see it differently.
If someone changes their mind in front of you, thank them rather than saying I told you so. Make it safe for everyone.
Today, hold off from sharing your opinion on something until you have asked two questions first.
Notice the difference between facts, values and preferences in a disagreement. Many arguments mix up all three.
Ask a friend with different politics, faith or background about how they came to their views. Listen for the story.
Being open-minded does not mean having no convictions. It means keeping them open to review.
Look back over the past month. Did you update a view, even slightly? Give yourself credit for it.
Notice when you look up information only to prove a point. Try searching for the opposing evidence instead.
Replace you are wrong with I see it differently. The change in tone changes what happens next.
Think about a decision at work you resisted that turned out well. What did you miss at the time?
Allow yourself to say, I do not know enough to have an opinion on that. It is a freeing sentence.
When you feel defensive, pause and breathe before you answer. A few seconds can turn a clash into a conversation.
Notice how often you assume the worst about people who think differently. Try imagining a good reason they might hold their view.
Write down one belief you would like to test this month. What evidence would you look for?
Changing your mind in private is easier than in public. Practise first in a journal, then with a trusted friend.
Listen to a long interview or podcast with someone whose views you dislike. Look for one point of common ground.
Notice the words always and never in your thinking. They often signal a closed door.
Halfway there. What is one view you now hold more loosely than when you began?
Ask someone younger and someone older than you for their take on the same question. Compare the answers.
When a new idea makes you uneasy, sit with the feeling for a day before rejecting it.
Practise the phrase, you may be right. It keeps a conversation open without forcing agreement.
Notice whether you change your mind more easily with some people than others. What makes them easier to hear?
Pride often blocks a change of heart. Remind yourself that updating a view is a sign of strength.
Try arguing the other side of a debate with a friend, just for fun. It stretches your thinking.
Pay attention to how you talk about people who disagree with you when they are not in the room.
If you made a strong claim and later learnt more, go back and say so. Corrections build trust.
Notice how certain your social feeds make you feel. Certainty spreads easily; nuance takes effort.
Before you share something online, ask whether you would still share it if it turned out to be only half true.
Think of one person whose opinion changed yours for the better. Thank them, if you can.
Open-mindedness includes being open to yourself. Allow your own tastes and plans to change as you grow.
When a plan you love is criticised, look for the useful part of the criticism before you defend it.
Notice the questions you are afraid to ask because the answer might unsettle you. Ask one gently.
Visit a place, event or group you would normally avoid, with genuine curiosity rather than judgement.
Practise saying, I have changed my mind, in a low-stakes setting, such as where to eat or which film to watch.
Remember that most people hold their views for reasons that make sense to them. Find those reasons.
Ask yourself whether you are disagreeing with the idea or with the person saying it.
When you learn you were mistaken, notice the relief as well as the sting. Letting go of a wrong idea lightens you.
Keep a small list titled things I used to think. Add to it as your views shift.
Notice how rigid views can strain relationships. A softer stance on a small matter might ease one at home.
Try leaving a disagreement unresolved. Not every difference needs to end in agreement.
Read a book that challenges something you care about. Underline the parts that make you think, not only the parts you dislike.
Pay attention to your tone when you share an opinion. Speaking with openness invites others to do the same.
When someone explains something you already know, listen anyway. They might add a detail you missed.
Notice when changing your mind feels like losing. Reframe it as gaining something you did not have before.
Ask a colleague, what am I not seeing here? Then really consider their answer.
Think about the opinions you inherited from family. Which have you examined, and which simply arrived with you?
Open-minded people are often better company. Notice how your conversations have changed recently.
Practise holding two ideas at once: I believe this, and I might be wrong.
Look for news that complicates a story you thought you understood. Complexity is often closer to the truth.
If you catch yourself mocking an opposing view, stop and restate it kindly instead.
Notice whether your certainty is based on evidence, habit or belonging. All three feel the same from the inside.
Model graceful change for those around you. When children or junior colleagues see you update a view, they learn it is safe.
Think of a view you have changed during these weeks. Tell someone about it and what changed your mind.
Being willing to be wrong makes you easier to trust. People know you are listening for the truth, not just your side.
Look at the topics you once avoided discussing. Is there one you could now explore calmly?
When you disagree, aim to leave the other person feeling heard, even if neither of you shifts.
Notice how much lighter conversations feel when you are not defending every position.
Ask yourself which of your current beliefs you would be most surprised to see change in ten years.
Gracefully changing your mind sometimes means saying sorry for how you argued before. Consider whether you owe one.
Keep reading, listening and asking. An open mind is kept open by steady curiosity.
Notice a habit of thought you have softened lately, perhaps a snap judgement about strangers. Small shifts like that add up.
Notice the people who now come to you to think things through. Openness draws others in.
Choose the habits you want to keep: asking before telling, rating your certainty, the list of things you used to think.
Think about how you will respond the next time a strongly held view is challenged. You have more tools now.
Share one of your changed views with someone who knew you before. Let them see you growing.
Remember that you can be open and still kind, open and still principled. These qualities fit together.
Look back over these ninety days. Which conversation shifted your thinking the most?
You started by noticing how certain you felt. Now you can hold your views with both conviction and humility.
Being able to change your mind is a kind of freedom. You are no longer trapped by what you once thought.
This is the last note. You have become someone who can listen, learn and change course gracefully, and that openness will keep growing with you.
